title: Man. Post. Cap. V: Contendo not our sin; Cap. 2 antecedent/consequent; judicial
pass_a_gloss: Be that as it may, my contention is that Adam's actual sin is not our sin, and therefore cannot justly be imputed to us. I admit that to impute is to assign, attribute, or charge to someone's account; yet several points must be kept in view here. Chief among them is the Cap. 2 distinction of imputation into antecedent and consequent—that is, immediate and mediate—which I set out when I fixed the state of the question and will not restate now; please keep it in mind. Further, what should stand before our thought is that we are dealing not with imputation in any loose sense, but with judicial imputation, the kind that a just punishment follows.
pass_b_english: But, whatever the case, I contend that that actual sin of Adam is not our sin. Therefore it cannot justly be imputed to us. I grant that to impute is to ascribe, to attribute, to write to one's account: but certain things are to be observed in this place—first of all that distinction of imputation into antecedent and consequent, or immediate and mediate, which, when I was setting the state of the question, I explained in Cap. 2, and do not repeat here: I ask you to remember it. Next this also ought to meet our thought: that what is in dispute between us is not any imputation whatever, but a judicial one, which just punishment follows.
source_text: Sed, quicquid sit, Contendo peccatum illud Adami actuale nostrum peccatum non esse. Itaque nobis jure imputari non posse. Fateor imputare esse tribuere, attribuere, adscribere: sed quaedam sunt hoc loco observanda, in primis distinctio illa imputationis in antecedentem & consequentem seu immediatam & mediatam, quam, dum statum quaestionis constituerem, Cap. 2. explicavi, nec hic repeto: ejus ut memineris te rogo. Deinde illud etiam cogitationi nostrae obversari debet, agi inter nos de imputatione non qualibet, sed judiciaria, quam punitio justa sequatur.
